body.p: Ovat Iki. There was another small town near a large, wide river in some Khanty town. It turns out that the Khanty also go hunting. And then a Khanty, a snowball fell, he had a wooden house in the forest, a hunting lodge. He also went to this hunting lodge, pulling a sledge behind him. It happens at home, on the hunt. Once he was hunting in winter. One day the snow melted and the swamps were left without snow, it had been there for so long. So he pulls the sledge and sets off. One day he came to a great swamp, in a great swamp, what it is - [that] is shown, [that] disappears. What kind of evil (contemptuous) man is he again? He pulled his little sledge behind him and drove there. What is that? As it turns out, Grandma Menk has failed. He made a big wooden hammer out of larch wood, dragged this hammer, he went to her, pulled out his grandmother Menk, hit her on the head. He pulled her up a little, hit her whole body with this hammer, Grandma Menk became like soft cloudberries. The poor old grandmother used to pick cranberries. She got stuck in the swamp. It turns out that she drowned in some open pits. Then he somehow cut along this grandmother's skin, shook it out so hard that the battered [body] became just like soft cloudberries, it turns out. Then he put on the coat of a big grandmother, went ahead, the grandmother who came. He came home there, he came home, and it turned out that she had two children. When he entered, they said: "Our mother has come. They stuck to me, stuck to my chest. He breastfed her. They sucked something nasty out of his chest, fell on their backs, poor two children. A little later her old man came, somewhere, was probably hunting, was probably [hunting], went, her farmer, a farmer in woolen clothes. [The Khanty in grandmother's clothes] shouted: Two of my children, while I was getting berries, cranberries, two of my children died, as it turned out. That night they do not sleep, on the third night he says to his husband: - You go to bed and I will keep watch that night. So he guards them. The man began to snore. As it turned out, there was a huge axe handle near the door, as wide as a [reindeer] hide. He chopped off the man's neck again with an axe. That's the way things are! Then dawn came, he didn't care about it. He went out into the street, grabbed that sledge with animal skins again and set off for the town. He came into the town, it was getting dark, it was already dawning, the town dogs wouldn't let him into the town. They bite him, they follow him. There is no way to enter the town. And he has to go back into the forest before it gets dark again, he sits down. He leaves again, the dogs don't recognize him. He can't take off her grandmother's clothes. They clung to his body. Again he tries to take it off, [but] can't take it off. It is completely connected to the skin of his body. [Town dwellers] live like this, they think: "These are our dogs, they can even see them." The Khanty will see him, they will only look out from behind the houses. He doesn't come into the tow. And he says: "I probably do, so I'm definitely not coming into town." Well, he left. He walks along the river, walks, suddenly he finds a large river chapel, he finally finds a river chapel, a large larch chapel, he builds himself a house there. So he lives in this [house] of his, only there are no fish. Some kind of inferior muzzle will be dipped, what kind of fish will it be. She goes to the Kazym woman and says: - This river is fishless, make fish for us. He goes to the man from the upper reaches of the river, the man from the upper reaches of the river says: - Why did you kill these women and men who bring good luck? Now you want fish. If you want fish, make your own fish if you need fish. What should he do, he went back into this house, lives, once, there was some kind of axe, hewn, throws his shavings into the water, looks, sees - uh, fish disappear quickly. Yes, then he lowered the muzzle - there are lots of fish. The rivers have now become fishy. He lives in this place all the time, he settles down. He is the one about whom they say [that this is] Owat Iki. He has become Owat Iki. For every animal, for every fish, he began to distribute happiness, began to show. Here is the end. Now he is probably still sitting on this high cape of his river. Everything, it's over.
